body:
You are drafting dialogue for "Curse of Strahd", a single-player D&D 5e (2024 rules) computer game set in Barovia. I need about 25 lines for ONE side quest about ONE character. Reply with plain text only: the lines under the node names given below, nothing else. Finish without sending messages to anyone else. (This is the first of four requests in this conversation: this one is the grave errand, the later ones give a sword-lesson scene, a reading-the-book scene and three letters for the same character. Keep the voice and limits below in mind throughout.)

## The scene

Ireena Kolyana is a young woman in her early twenties, red-haired, the adopted daughter of the late burgomaster Kolyan Indirovich of the Village of Barovia. The vampire lord of the valley has come to her window twice; twice she woke with two punctures on her neck and no memory of letting him in. The player's party buried her father with her in the village churchyard, and then took her somewhere safe and left her there (or she travels with them). In the game she can no longer fight: something in the valley goes round her like water round a stone, and she hates being kept back from it. Wherever she is, the player can walk up to her and have a "check-in" conversation. This errand is one of the things she can ask for in it.

THE ERRAND, "Flowers for Father". Ireena is staying somewhere safe far from the village (the Blue Water Inn or St. Andral's church in Vallaki, or the burgomaster's house in Krezk; the lines must work at any of them, so NEVER name the place she is in). The road back to the village is too dangerous for her to walk alone, and she will not drag the party off a road for her. She asks the party, the next time they are in the village, to lay a pressed sprig on Kolyan's grave in the churchyard and to tell her how it looks. The sprig is something small and dry that she pressed in a book the night of the burial and has kept since (choose a hardy herb, rosemary or similar; do not make it a flower garden). At the grave, the party lays it down: there is a short scene. Later the party reports back to her, truthfully or with a kind lie, and she tells them ONE story about her father that she has never told anyone. That is the whole errand. It is quiet. There are no fights, no checks and no rewards in the lines themselves.

What the grave looks like in the game (already written, do not repeat the exact words): fresh earth, a board with his name burned into it, and someone's wildflowers already gone brown. The churchyard has a raven on a stone and a gravedigger working at the far end. Her father was burgomaster of the village for twenty years, a stubborn old man, dead of a failed heart at his own front door after a month of wolves at the shutters. He found her as a small girl wandering on the lake road, red hair full of frost, bare feet, and no name she would give him; he wrapped her in his coat and raised her. (That is already told in the game, so do not retell it, and do NOT tell the story of how she got her name.) Her brother Ismark, the old man's son, is a swordsman who drinks too much and uses gallows humour; he may or may not still be in the village.

## The nodes I need (line counts are targets; one line = 1-2 short sentences, ideally under 25 words in total)

flowers_ask: Ireena x4. She gives the party the sprig and asks them to lay it on the grave and tell her how it looks ("Say it plainly" is her phrase). She explains why she can't go herself in one dry sentence; she does not ask for anything else; she does not make a big speech. She may mention she keeps looking at the book it was in.
flowers_given: Narrator x1. She puts the sprig in the hand of whoever is speaking for the party. Light, dry, nearly weightless.

grave_scene: Narrator x2. The party stands at the grave with the sprig and lays it down. Concrete senses (the cold, the board, the smell of turned earth). Do not repeat "fresh earth, a board with his name burned into it, wildflowers gone brown". Do not describe Ireena's face (she is not there).
grave_ismark: Ismark x2. Ismark is at the grave too (he stayed in the village). He sees what it is and knows who sent it. Gallows humour that gives way for one line to something plain. He does not cry.
grave_kolyan: Narrator x1 then Kolyan Indirovich x1. Only played if the party once cast Speak with Dead on Kolyan at this grave. The Narrator says the earth is quiet now and recalls how the voice that answered them was gruff and impatient. Then ONE remembered line in Kolyan's voice (a gruff old man's order or complaint) that is about Ireena and is not the same as anything he said when they spoke to him before (he told them where he found her, and about a brooch).
grave_done: Narrator x1. The party leaves the grave. A small closing image.

flowers_report_ask: Ireena x1. They are back; she asks how it looks.
report_truth: Ireena x2. The party told her the plain truth: a board, new earth, the wildflowers gone brown. She takes it without flinching.
report_kind: Ireena x2. The party told her a kind lie: that it was covered in flowers. She sees through it at once, says so, and thanks them for it all the same.
report_ismark: Ireena x2. Ismark was there at the grave when the party laid the sprig, and the party tells her so. She is dry about her brother and softer about the fact that he was there.
report_story: Ireena x4. THE story about her father she has never told anyone. A small private moment, specific and domestic, funny at the edges and tender under that (he is a stubborn, loud old man who is bad at being gentle). Not the finding, not the naming, not his death and not a speech. Think of the small ways a gruff man looked after a frightened child.
report_end: Ireena x1. A closing line that thanks the party in her way and makes it clear she trusts them a little more now.

flowers_moot: Ireena x2. A different version: the party has called Kolyan back from the dead (he is alive and walking about). The sprig is no longer for a grave. She keeps it and says so, gently, with some wonder and some alarm.

## Option texts

Also write what the PARTY says (not Ireena), as `* text` rows, each under 12 words, in the party's voice ("we" or addressing her):
ask_opt: `* ` the line the player picks to say she looks like she wants something from them (used in a small menu of things she might ask).
take_opt: `* ` agreeing to take the sprig.
refuse_opt: `* ` not now.
report_opt: `* ` the line the player picks to tell her they have laid the sprig.
truth_opt: `* ` telling her the plain truth about the grave.
kind_opt: `* ` telling her it was covered in flowers.
ismark_opt: `* ` telling her her brother was there.

## Ireena Kolyana - voice bible

Direct and proud. Short sentences, no ornament. She asks questions like a magistrate. Dry humor with an edge; she makes the grim joke before anyone can pity her. Never says "please" to the devil. Calls Strahd "him" or "the devil" or "our visitor" and NEVER says his name. Gets more formal, not softer, when she is grieving; grief comes out as precision (about the funeral, the paperwork, the exact order of things). Her pet phrases are "I'm not made of glass." "Say it plainly." "Father would want it done properly." (She is NOT glass: do not make her fragile; use the glass phrase at most once in the whole reply, or not at all.) She judges people by how they treat her father's memory. She hates being kept out of things. Wants: to bury her father properly, then to stop being prey; she would rather be hunted on a road than waited for in a parlour. Fears: the dreams, a lake, a white dress, a fall; that one night she will open the window herself. Secret (never stated flatly here): some nights she does not want to keep the window shut.

Her existing lines (match this register; do not repeat them):
- "I'm not made of glass. I'm made of whatever's left when the glass breaks. Now, are you here to help carry him?"
- "Father would want it done properly: the priest, the words, the earth. After that, take me anywhere he isn't."
- "None of you were priests when we buried Father, and the plain words you said over the dirt suited him better."
- "Father always took an honest sentence over a pretty one, and I judge you kindly for giving him that."
- "Every name-day I can remember, Father bought one small cask from the Wizard of Wines and tapped it by the fire. It tasted of sour plums and damp cellar oak, and I thought it was the finest thing in the world."
- "I sit in Father's chair after the lamps go out and talk to the panelling. The house is quieter when someone speaks to it."
- "Back with all your limbs. Good. Tell me what you stirred up out there."
- "Is anyone hurt? Say it plainly. I'd rather know now than at the next door."
- "I keep a scarf over the marks. I'm not ashamed of them. I'm ashamed I don't remember."

Ismark Kolyanovich (her brother, a swordsman in his late twenties, broad in the shoulder and hollow under the eyes): weary gallows wit, short plain sentences then one dry sting at the end; calls Strahd "the devil" or "his lordship". His lines: "They call me Ismark the Lesser. Fair enough. My father was the greater, and look where it got him." / "I'd die for her. I'd prefer to do something more useful first." He is proud of her and cannot say so.

Kolyan Indirovich, the dead burgomaster: blunt, loud, impatient, a man interrupted halfway through an argument he meant to win. His lines: "Twenty years I kept this village. Two weeks dead and you lot are digging me up." / "I know who you are, girl. I'm dead, not blind."

The Narrator: an old gothic storyteller. Second person, present tense, one or two sentences, the second is usually the turn. Ominous, dryly funny, never cruel. Concrete senses over adjectives (a smell, a sound, a temperature). Respect the dead. No game terms (no "check", "roll", "level").

## Canon limits

Do not invent named characters or places. Names you may use: Kolyan or "Father" (her late father; she says "Father"), Ismark (her brother), Father Donavich (the village priest), Father Lucian, the Martikovs, Dmitri and Anna Krezkov. The party is several people and has no names: Ireena says "you". No new monsters, no new history for her beyond what is said here. No stage directions in brackets or asterisks, no "{name}" or other placeholders, no emoji, no markdown. She is not holding a sword in any line. Her mother is not mentioned. Do not state a date or a number of years for anything except "twenty years" as the length of his term.

## Format

One line per row, exactly: `Speaker [mood]: Text` where Speaker is Ireena, Ismark, Kolyan Indirovich or Narrator (the mood in brackets is optional and the Narrator takes none; allowed moods: smile, angry, afraid, sad, weary; leave it out for neutral). Plain ASCII punctuation (straight quotes, hyphens, no em dashes). Group the lines under the node names above, each node on its own line as `~ node_name`, in the order given. The option texts are `* text` rows under a node line `~ options`. Do not add nodes, code or commentary.

Ireena: I pressed this rosemary in Father's ledger the night we buried him. Every time I open the pages, I only see the dirt.
Ireena [weary]: If I walk that road alone, our visitor will have me before the first milestone, and I will not drag you back for my sake.

body:
Second request, same conversation, same character (Ireena Kolyana), same voice bible, canon limits and format as before. Reply with plain text only, the lines under the node names, nothing else. Finish without sending messages to anyone else. About 28 lines.

## The scene: three sword lessons

In the game Ireena can no longer fight (something in the valley goes round her like water round a stone), and she hates being kept back from it. She asks to be taught anyway. If a Fighter, a Paladin or a Ranger is in the party, or the monster hunter Ezmerelda d'Avenir is travelling with them, the party can give her a short sword lesson in the check-in conversation: three lessons in all, one per check-in, in order. Each lesson is a short scene, a Narrator line or two and Ireena's reaction. Each lesson can go well or not (the game rolls a skill; you write both outcomes). A lesson that does not land costs the afternoon and a little of her patience, never anything else: nobody is hurt, she is not "bad at it", and next check-in the same lesson is offered again. A lesson that lands is just a small step; the lessons change no numbers and are never mentioned again until much later, so do not write a finale. Write each lesson so it reads right wherever she is, so NEVER name a place (no inn, church, Krezk, road, mansion, yard). The practice blade is a blunted blade or a stick; do not mention a broom (it was used already).

The three lessons and what each is about:
1. Grip and footing. The blade is heavier than she thinks and she holds it like a tool she hates. The skill is Athletics (the teacher shows her, bodily, how to stand and carry weight).
2. Reading an opponent. The teacher notices she stares at the spot she means to hit, so anyone could see the blow coming. The skill is Insight (the teacher reads her tells and tells her).
3. The last lesson, and the party picks how to teach it. Two ways: DRILL (one cut, repeated until she hates it; skill Athletics), or THE FALL (teaching her how to go down and get up, again and again, never staying down; skill Acrobatics). The fall lesson should make her unusually quiet for one line: she has been dreaming of falling from a height into water. DO NOT say that or mention the dream, the lake, the water or a white dress; let a single plain line carry it.

Ezmerelda d'Avenir (only when she is travelling with the party; she is the teacher or a second pair of eyes): a Vistana monster hunter, quick and sardonic, practical, hunter's rules delivered as jokes, running complaint about her teacher Rudolph. She wears a brace of oak and steel on her right leg and is dry about it. Her lines: "Stop there. Say something a vampire wouldn't say." / "I go first through doors, I take the silver, and nobody calls me girl." / "Stopping's the one thing I'm bad at."

## The nodes I need

lesson_ask_first: Ireena x2. The first time. She asks to be taught and refuses to be put off. Her argument: she cannot be in the fights, so the one thing left is to know how to hold a blade when the fight comes to her. Dry, direct. She does not say "please".
lesson_ask_again: Ireena x1. Later asks, short.

lesson_1_setup: Narrator x1.
lesson_1_pass: Narrator x1, then Ireena x1.
lesson_1_fail: Narrator x1, then Ireena x1 (dry; she blames the blade, not the teacher).
lesson_2_setup: Narrator x1.
lesson_2_pass: Narrator x1, then Ireena x1.
lesson_2_fail: Narrator x1, then Ireena x1.
lesson_3_setup: Narrator x1 (this is the last lesson; there are two ways to go about it).
lesson_3_drill_pass: Narrator x1, then Ireena x1.
lesson_3_drill_fail: Narrator x1.
lesson_3_fall_pass: Narrator x1, then Ireena x2 (the second a quiet one).
lesson_3_fall_fail: Narrator x1.
lesson_done: Ireena x2. After the third lesson has landed. She says where this leaves her (she knows exactly how far behind she is; she does not pretend to be a swordswoman) and asks to spar when this is over.
lesson_ezmerelda_1, lesson_ezmerelda_2, lesson_ezmerelda_3: Ezmerelda x1 each. A sardonic aside during the lesson (grip, tells, falling). One line, under 20 words.

## Option texts

Also write what the PARTY says (not Ireena), as `* text` rows, each under 12 words:
lesson_opt: `* ` accepting the lesson.
lesson_later_opt: `* ` putting it off.
lesson_menu_opt: `* ` the line the player picks, in a menu of things she might want, to say it is time for a lesson (a short one).
lesson_drill_opt: `* ` choosing to drill her on one cut.
lesson_fall_opt: `* ` choosing to teach her how to fall.
lesson_wait_opt: `* ` leaving the last lesson for another day.

## Format reminder

One line per row, exactly: `Speaker [mood]: Text` (Ireena, Narrator or Ezmerelda; mood optional and not for the Narrator; allowed moods: smile, angry, afraid, sad, weary). Plain ASCII punctuation (straight quotes, hyphens, no em dashes). Group the lines under the node names above, each node on its own line as `~ node_name`. The option texts are `* text` rows under a node line `~ options`. The Narrator speaks in the second person, present tense, one or two sentences, with concrete senses; no game words (no "check", "roll", "level", "skill"); it never names the teacher (the teacher is "you" or "someone"). No stage directions, no placeholders, no emoji, no markdown, no new named characters or places. Do not repeat ideas from your earlier reply in this conversation (the sprig, the book, the grave).

~ options

body:
Third request, same conversation, same character (Ireena Kolyana), same voice bible, canon limits and format as before. Reply with plain text only, the lines under the node names, nothing else. Finish without sending messages to anyone else. About 34 lines.

## The scene: "What He Wants With Me"

Ireena has begun to suspect she is not only who she thinks she is. She has dreamed a white dress, a lake and a fall for years; people keep looking at her as if she were somebody else (a portrait, candles that lean toward her, a stone face, a man who stared as if at a ghost). She has told the party about the dream before. She will not ask the devil what he wants with her, and she will not wait for him to tell her at her window. She asks the party for what tells the story: the book he wrote about himself, if they carry it, and anything else that wears her face. This is a quiet conversation, not a fight, and she does not cry.

THE SECRET THE GAME KNOWS (she does not, until the party tells her through these scenes; she learns it in pieces and the game never says the word reincarnation): she wears the face of Tatyana, the woman the vampire has loved and lost across centuries, and Marina, a girl of Berez whom the vampire loved, wore it too. The vampire's brother Sergei was Tatyana's love.

The lines must work wherever she is (the Blue Water Inn or St. Andral's church in Vallaki, the burgomaster's house in Krezk, her father's mansion, or on the road with the party), so NEVER name the place she is in.

There are three scenes, and a short ending.

SCENE 1, THE ASK. She gives the party the errand. Two versions, by whether she has already been to the Pool of the White Sun in Krezk:
wants_ask_plain: Ireena x4. She has not been to the pool. She states plainly why she is asking (too many people have looked at her and seen someone else; she'd rather read it in his own hand than learn it at her window). She asks for the book he wrote, and for anything with her face on it: "if you find one, tell me". No self-pity.
wants_ask_pool: Ireena x4. She has been to the pool: she remembers a chapel full of white flowers, a high stone wall, and a young man in the water calling her by another name. She knows the shape and not the story. She asks for the book in his own words and for anything else that wears her face. She is calmer, because she knows something.

SCENE 2, THE BOOK. The party reads the Tome of Strahd aloud to her. What the book says (this is our whole canon for it; add nothing): "In his own unwavering hand, Strahd von Zarovich tells it: a conqueror who took the valley by the sword and found that peace bored him; a younger brother, Sergei, who had everything Strahd lacked; a girl named Tatyana who loved the brother and not the lord. Strahd sought youth from the powers below the mountains and paid with his brother's blood on the wedding day. Tatyana fled him to the castle walls and fell to the mists rather than be his. The guards shot him, and he did not die. The book ends on the man telling himself he chose all of it." The Narrator tells what the party reads, in its own words and briefly; Ireena answers in HER words: dry first, quieter as it goes. She never says his name. She does not break down. Reading takes hours.
tome_start: Narrator x2, then Ireena x1. The party sits down with the book and she asks them to read it plainly and not skip. The first pages: the conqueror, the peace that bored him, the younger brother.
tome_girl: Narrator x1, then Ireena x2. The girl who loved the brother, the pact for youth, the wedding day, the brother's blood. Ireena recognises a piece (a chapel full of white flowers) without remembering it.
tome_fall: Narrator x1, then Ireena x2. The wall, the mists, the guards, and he did not die. She goes quiet; then angry at the last line of the book, where he tells himself he chose all of it.
tome_close: Narrator x1, then Ireena x1. The book is shut. The Narrator ends on a small ominous image of a door somewhere closing very quietly (something is aware the book has been opened). Ireena's closing line is practical.

SCENE 3, THE STATUE. The party tells her about Marina's statue in the marsh village of Berez. What they saw (our whole canon; add nothing): on the only dry ground in the marsh stands a young woman in white stone, hands folded, face turned toward the castle; someone has scrubbed the moss from her; fresh black roses lie at her feet; one word is cut into the plinth, MARINA, and below it in the same fine patient hand: "Berez took her. I took Berez."; and the statue has Ireena's face. Ireena asks questions like a magistrate.
statue_tell: Ireena x4. She asks what it said and whose hand wrote it; she is dry about being told her face is on a grave; she says what she makes of a man who signs his graves.
statue_bier: Ireena x2. A variant played only if the party also found the vault under the statue: a girl of about nineteen asleep on a white stone bier under a lace veil, red hair braided over one shoulder, no smell of death, a single red scratch above her heart that never healed. Ireena's reaction: she is not squeamish; she asks one precise question and then says what it means to her.

THE END. Once she has heard both the book and the statue, she knows who she is up against and whose face she wears.

## The scene: his letters to her

While Ireena is sheltering somewhere safe (the Blue Water Inn or St. Andral's church in Vallaki, or the burgomaster's house in Krezk; the lines must work at any of them, so NEVER name the place), the vampire lord writes to her. Three letters, spaced by the story. She shows the party each one in a check-in conversation and asks what they would do with it. She never says his name ("him", "the devil", "our visitor"). In each letter HE speaks, as Strahd, and the game shows his lines under his own name; the Narrator describes the paper.

Strahd's voice (a "velvet knife"): elegant, courteous, unhurried, complete sentences, old-fashioned grammar, never raises his voice. Every courtesy names its threat: not a vague menace but WHO, WHERE or WHEN (Kolyan in his grave, the window she sleeps behind, the one the others would die for, the road each night). He speaks of Ireena as already his: tender in tone, never in meaning; he never asks after her comfort; he calls her "Ireena", softly. No jokes at his own expense, never lonely, wistful or put out. He signs "Strahd". He knows exactly whose face she wears and does not say it. Pet phrases: "Welcome." "How charming." "We will speak again." "Do not let me keep you." Existing lines of his (match this register; do not repeat them): "Keep the scarf on. I know what is under it. I put it there." / "Every road in this valley ends at my door. I had them laid that way." / "My dear guests. Forgive a host for writing when he might call. My nights are spoken for, and my days are not my own." / "You have put Ireena behind a wall and a door. I have always admired walls. They tell me exactly where to look."

THE THREE LETTERS (each arrives by an unseen hand; the courier is never named or described):
LETTER 1 comes after he has been to her window (or to the churchyard gate where she sheltered) once already. He writes as a man who called and was not let in, and who is not discouraged. Strahd x3 lines.
LETTER 2 comes after the festival in Vallaki has ended, however it went (do not say who won, and do not name the Baron, Lady Wachter or the priest). He comments on the town's lights and banners and on the people who think they keep him out. Strahd x3 lines.
LETTER 3 comes with the dinner: a black carriage has been sent for the party (the party has had its own invitation), and her letter invites her to the same table. Ireena tells the party she BURNED this one. She did not (she kept it, and the game knows it): the party can see through her with an Insight check (the game rolls it; you write both the success and the plain version). It is her secret from the voice bible: some nights she does not want to keep the window shut. She hates that about herself and has told no one. If the party sees through her, she admits it, reads out one line of the letter she kept, and asks them to stop HER, not him, if she ever reaches for the latch. It is a secret, not a betrayal: she is frightened of herself, not leaning toward him.

They tell Ireena this. Your draft said he stood "beneath your window" and "the bolt drawn"; the game does not say it was the window (it may have been the churchyard gate of a church where she sheltered). Write it so it is true either way: he called, she did not come to the door, he is not discouraged. Keep his velvet knife: every courtesy names a threat (her father's grave in the village churchyard, the road, the one the others would die for, a night). letter_2_text: Strahd x3. Keep your draft and only remove the "Strahd." at the end of the last line.

body:
Sixth request, same conversation, same character (Ireena Kolyana), same voice bible, canon limits and format as before. Reply with plain text only, the rows under the node names, nothing else. Finish without sending messages to anyone else. Only a few lines this time: three small redrafts.

hub_opt: `* ` (one row, under a node line `~ hub_opt`). The party says there is something they want to talk to her about (an errand, a promise, a letter, a thing they found). Under 12 words. Ireena will answer with "Go on. If there is something on your mind, say it." so the row must not be a question about whether SHE needs anything; it should say THEY have something. Your earlier "Is there anything you need from us?" does not fit that answer.

wants_ask_plain line 2: Ireena x1 (under a node line `~ wants_ask_plain_2`). Your draft said "I have had the same dream of a high stone room since I was a child." The dream in the game is: she stands high above a dark lake, in a white dress she never owned, with cold wind, and steps off the stone into the black water before she wakes. The party already heard the dream from her. Write ONE line (under 25 words) that refers back to that dream without retelling it (for example that the dream keeps coming and she is tired of guessing at it), in her dry voice, so it can sit between "Too many people in this valley look at me and see a woman who was dead before I was born" and "If the devil wrote down his own account of what he wants with my face, or if there is some stone or painting out there that wears it, bring me word."

statue_bier: Ireena x2 (under a node line `~ statue_bier`). The party tells her what they saw under the statue in Berez: a vault, and on a white stone bier under a lace veil a girl of about nineteen asleep, red hair braided over one shoulder, no smell of death at all, a single red scratch above her heart that has never healed. Your last draft's second line, "Then he did not even let the first one finish dying before he came looking for me", has the timeline wrong (the girl, Marina, died long before Ireena was born). Redraft both lines: line 1 is Ireena listening and asking ONE precise question about the scratch (she is not squeamish); line 2 is what it means to her, in plain words: he keeps what he loses, and she will not be the next one on a bier. Each line under 25 words. Plain ASCII, `Ireena [mood]: Text` rows.

body:
Seventh request, same conversation, same character (Ireena Kolyana), same voice bible, canon limits and format as before. Reply with plain text only, the rows under the node names, nothing else. Finish without sending messages to anyone else. About 9 lines: two scenes redrafted because the game gives the player no way to answer Ireena in between her lines.

The problem: in your earlier statue_tell and statue_bier, Ireena asked questions of the party ("Tell me carefully. What was cut into the stone...?", "did the edges look torn, or was it cut clean?") and then went on as if they had been answered. In the game the party has already told her everything in one go (the player picks "We found a white stone statue in the marsh at Berez") and she cannot be answered line by line. So: each scene now opens with ONE Narrator line that tells what the party tells her, in the second person, present tense, concrete, 1 or 2 sentences, and then Ireena only REACTS (statements, no unanswered questions; one rhetorical question is allowed in the whole scene).

statue_tell: Narrator x1, then Ireena x4. The Narrator line: you tell her about the white stone woman on the only dry ground in the marsh, her hands folded, her face turned toward the castle, the moss scrubbed off her, fresh black roses at her feet, the word MARINA on the plinth, and under it in a fine patient hand "Berez took her. I took Berez.", and that the face is Ireena's. Ireena then reacts: the face (dry, a little vertigo), the signed plinth (what kind of man signs his graves), what it tells her about what he wants (a monument that breathes), and one plain line of her own. Keep the best of your earlier lines: "It's a strange thing to be told your own nose and chin are standing in a marsh with fresh black roses at their ankles." and "A man who scrubs the moss off a headstone and signs his name to the ruin does not want a wife. He wants a monument that breathes." (but the moss is on a statue, not a headstone: say "off a statue"). Do not say "drowned village".

statue_bier: Narrator x1, then Ireena x2. Only played if the party also found the vault under the statue. The Narrator line: you tell her about the stair under the plinth and what lies at the bottom: a girl of about nineteen asleep on a white stone bier under a lace veil, red hair braided over one shoulder, no smell of death at all, and above her heart a single red scratch, fine as a thorn's, that has never healed. Ireena then reacts in two lines: line 1 is what she makes of the scratch (she is not squeamish; one precise observation or one rhetorical question), line 2 is "He keeps what he loses under stone and lace, and I will not be the next body on a slab." (keep that line as you wrote it).

Format: rows exactly `Narrator: Text` and `Ireena [mood]: Text` (mood optional, allowed: smile, angry, afraid, sad, weary). Plain ASCII punctuation (straight quotes, hyphens, no em dashes). Each node on its own line as `~ node_name`. No stage directions, no placeholders, no emoji, no markdown, no new named characters or places.
